h1:
Samut Songkhram 3 Days 2 Nights
Amphawa, Don Hoi Lot & Riverside Temples
intro: Samut Songkhram is Thailand's smallest province, but it packs in far more to do than you'd expect. It's barely over an hour's drive from Bangkok, and once you arrive you'll find a market built across a railway track, floating markets, old temples along the Mae Klong River, and fresh seafood from the Don Hoi Lot sandbar. Three days and two nights is just the right amount of time — enough to take it slow without rushing, and to see several different sides of Maeklong town in one trip.

blocks.html: This plan is built for travelers who want to see Samut Songkhram properly without wearing themselves out. It tackles one zone at a time so you're not driving back and forth. Day one stays in Maeklong town, day two covers the Amphawa side along with the riverside temples, and day three wraps up at the Don Hoi Lot sandbar and the mudflats of Khlong Khon. The trip works best as a Friday–Sunday getaway, since the Amphawa floating market and firefly boat trips only run on Fridays, Saturdays and Sundays.

blocks.title: Read this before you plan
blocks.html: The Amphawa floating market and firefly boat tours open only on Friday, Saturday and Sunday. Fireflies show up best in the rainy season (May–October) and on moonless nights. If you're traveling on a weekday, it's worth shuffling the plan so your Amphawa day lands on the weekend.

blocks.text: Day 1 — Maeklong town, the train market and Wat Phet Samut

blocks.html: Day one stays in town the whole day. The highlight is the Maeklong train market, a fresh market that sits right across the Maeklong railway line. As a train approaches, the vendors fold up their awnings and pull their goods back from the track in a flash, then set everything out again the moment the train has passed. It's a scene known around the world, and people photograph it nonstop.

items.activity: Leave Bangkok and drive down via Rama II Road; Maeklong is about 1.5 hours away
items.note: By van, there's a Bangkok–Maeklong line from the new Southern Bus Terminal

items.activity: Walk the train market and catch the rhythm of trains coming and going, with snacks along the way
items.note: Trains pass about 8 times a day; the midday slots are 11:10 and 11:30

items.activity: Lunch in Maeklong market — try the short, bent-necked Maeklong mackerel, the province's signature catch
items.note: Steamed in its basket, Maeklong mackerel is firm and richer than elsewhere

items.activity: Pay respects to Luang Pho Ban Laem at Wat Phet Samut Worawihan, the town's landmark temple
items.note: Open daily, free entry

items.activity: Settle into a cafe on the Mae Klong River in town for coffee while the boats drift by
items.note: The Maeklong riverside has several newly opened cafes

items.activity: Check in to your stay around Amphawa and get ready for the next day
items.note: Staying in Amphawa for both nights beats moving hotels

blocks.title: Train market tip
blocks.html: For a good shot of the awnings folding down, stake out your spot about 10 minutes before the train arrives and frame the head of the track. It's busiest in the late morning and afternoon. Mind your valuables — the lane is narrow and the crowd is tight.

blocks.text: Day 2 — Amphawa, riverside temples and the firefly boat ride

blocks.html: This is the heart of the trip. In the morning you'll visit two very different temples on the Mae Klong River; in the afternoon you'll relax at the Rama II Memorial Park; in the evening you'll walk the Amphawa floating market for good food, then finish with a firefly boat ride after dark — the one thing many people come to Amphawa specifically to do.

items.activity: Head to Wat Bang Kung to see the Bot Prok Pho, an old ordination hall completely wrapped in the roots of a giant bodhi tree
items.note: The grounds also have the Bang Kung Camp and boxer statues to walk around

items.activity: Stop at Wat Bang Khae Noi to see an ordination hall whose teakwood walls are carved with the life of the Buddha throughout — woodwork you rarely come across
items.note: It sits on the Mae Klong River, close to the Amphawa route

items.activity: Lunch at a riverside restaurant around Amphawa — order grilled river prawns and fried mackerel
items.note: The spots along the Amphawa canal have nice views; book a waterside table ahead on weekends

items.activity: Walk the King Rama II Memorial Park to see the traditional Thai houses and the garden of plants from classical literature
items.note: Open daily 08:30–17:00 (until 17:30 on weekends)

items.activity: Walk the Amphawa floating market and graze along the canal — fried oyster omelet, boat noodles, coconut sweets
items.note: The market runs Friday–Sunday, roughly 10:00–20:30

items.activity: Take a boat to see fireflies along the Mae Klong River, watching the lamphu trees sparkle
items.note: About 500 THB to charter a whole boat (seats around 10), or roughly 50–60 THB per person on a shared one

blocks.title: What to know about the fireflies
blocks.html: Fireflies are living creatures — they aren't out in the same numbers every night. Moonless nights in the rainy season are when you'll see the most; on a full moon or in the dry season there may be few. It's a natural thing nobody can control, and we'll be straight with you so you don't go in expecting too much.

If you've still got energy after the boat ride, the Amphawa floating market keeps buzzing past 9 pm — you can do another loop of snacks along the canal. The nighttime riverside has a charm of its own that the daytime doesn't.

blocks.text: Day 3 — Don Hoi Lot, the mudflats and seafood

blocks.html: The last day heads for the coast. Don Hoi Lot is the sandbar at the mouth of the Mae Klong River that emerges as a wide mudflat when the tide goes out, with razor clams buried under the sand. At low tide, locals go out to coax the clams up for you to watch — a way of life that's hard to find elsewhere. Before heading back to Bangkok, stop for fresh seafood and grab some local treats to take home.

items.activity: Check out and drive to Don Hoi Lot; look up the tide table before you set off
items.note: Only at low tide will you see the sandbar and the razor clams

items.activity: Walk the Don Hoi Lot sandbar, watch the clam-coaxing, and pay respects at the Krom Luang Chumphon shrine by the shore
items.note: Wear shoes you don't mind getting wet — the ground is muddy

items.activity: Lunch at a seafood restaurant around Don Hoi Lot — try stir-fried razor clams with herbs, fried mackerel, and red curry with sea blite leaves
items.note: Well-known spots include Khun Pao Don Hoi Lot and the canalside restaurants nearby

items.activity: Head to the Khlong Khon Mangrove Conservation Center to try planting mangroves or take a boat through the mangrove forest
items.note: It's a conservation activity — call ahead to book

items.activity: Pick up souvenirs — real coconut sugar, baskets of steamed mackerel, large white-fleshed pomelos — before you go
items.note: Maeklong coconut sugar is fragrant and isn't bleached
Avoid the Sunday-evening crush, when traffic often jams heading into the city

blocks.text: Optional swaps if you have time or want to adjust

blocks.html: The plan above sticks to the main highlights, but Samut Songkhram has other corners you can swap in depending on your interests. If you like traditional floating markets that aren't overrun yet, or want to see how coconut sugar is made, pick from this list to replace anything that doesn't grab you.

items.name: Tha Kha Floating Market
items.blurb: A traditional floating market set among the orchards, open only on certain days. The mood is simpler than Amphawa — good for anyone after some quiet.

items.name: Coconut sugar farm
items.blurb: Watch the old-school way of tapping the palms and boiling down coconut sugar, and taste it fresh — a nice stop to bring kids along to learn.

items.name: Wat Bang Kung & Bang Kung Camp
items.blurb: Beyond the bodhi-root ordination hall, there's Thonburi-era history here to walk through.

items: Match your dates to the floating market — Amphawa and the firefly boats run Friday–Sunday, so if you want the full experience, make day two fall on the weekend.
Check the tide table — Don Hoi Lot only reveals its sandbar at low tide, so check before you set your day-three timing.
Stay in Amphawa both nights — no need to switch hotels, and you'll have easy access to the floating market and the firefly boats.
Bring cash — the floating market, the train market and many firefly boat operators take mostly cash.
Leave a buffer for the drive home — Sunday evenings, Rama II Road heading into Bangkok tends to jam; setting off before 3 pm is more comfortable.

faq.q: Where should I stay for a 3-day, 2-night Samut Songkhram trip?
faq.a: Staying around Amphawa for both nights is the easiest, since it's close to the floating market and the firefly boat launch, so you don't have to move hotels mid-trip. Options range from canalside homestays to resorts on the Mae Klong River.

faq.q: What days are the Amphawa floating market and firefly boats open?
faq.a: The Amphawa floating market opens only on Friday, Saturday and Sunday, roughly 10:00–20:30. The firefly boat rides run on those same nights, setting off in the evening after sunset. Fireflies are clearest in the rainy season and on moonless nights.

faq.q: Do I need to check the tides for Don Hoi Lot?
faq.a: Yes. Don Hoi Lot only shows its sandbar and razor clams at low tide. Go at high tide and it's just open sea with no mudflat in sight. Check that day's tide table before you set your departure time.

faq.q: How long is the drive from Bangkok to Samut Songkhram?
faq.a: It's about 1.5 hours via Rama II Road if traffic is light — one of the closest provinces to Bangkok, good for both a weekend trip and a longer one. If you're not driving, there are Bangkok–Maeklong vans you can take.

faq.q: What souvenirs are Samut Songkhram known for?
faq.a: The local favorites are real coconut sugar that's fragrant and unbleached, steamed Maeklong mackerel in its basket, large white-fleshed pomelos, and sweets made from coconut sugar. You'll find them around Maeklong market, the Amphawa floating market, and the roadside shops near Don Hoi Lot.
